passage:
'You're here again?' Pooja asked, finding Irfan on the library steps at lunch.
'Where else? Rehan's lot said the table's full. It's always full.'
'You're still trying to sit with them?'
'I thought if I got good at football...' He shrugged. 'I'm not.'
Pooja pointed at the sketchbook on his knee. 'Is that a kingfisher?'
'Common kingfisher. I saw it at the lake on Sunday. The colours were ridiculous.'
'We've got a bird-count group. Saturdays, six in the morning, by the lake. Four of us and one pair of binoculars we fight over.'
'Six? In the morning?'
'The birds don't wait for you to wake up.' She grinned. 'Bring the sketchbook. Nobody in the group can draw.'
Irfan turned a page. 'I've got a heron too.'
'Then you're definitely coming.'
On Saturday he was at the lake at ten to six.

qa.q: Which bird had Irfan drawn that he saw at the lake on Sunday?
qa.a: He had drawn a common kingfisher, and he had a heron too.

qa.q: What does Irfan's 'I thought if I got good at football...' reveal about how he had been feeling?
qa.a: It shows he had been trying hard to earn a place with Rehan's lot and felt deflated and left out when it didn't work.

qa.q: Why is the bird-count group a better turning point than chasing Rehan's table?
qa.a: It is built around something Irfan already loves, so he can belong by doing and sharing his drawings instead of trying to win over a crowd that keeps saying the table is full.

qa.q: How does Pooja see Irfan's sketchbook?
qa.a: Pooja sees it as something the group is missing, since nobody there can draw, so inviting him feels like gaining a member rather than doing a favour.

grounding: It shows a left-out teen finding belonging in a small group built around a shared interest rather than chasing the popular crowd.

passage:
Last term, when my old group started sitting with the girls from 10B, I spent weeks trying to squeeze back in. I laughed at jokes I didn't get. I bought the same keychain. Nothing changed; I was still the one at the end of the bench.
Then I saw the notice: 'Backstage crew needed for annual play. No acting. Paint, glue, hammers.'
Raghav, who ran it, handed me a brush on the first day and said, 'Vidya, the forest needs more trees.' That was it. No test.
For three weeks we painted, argued about shades of green and ate samosas on dust sheets. Nobody had to be interesting. We just had to finish the forest.
I still see my old group in the corridor. It stings less now. I've got somewhere to be at four.

qa.q: What did the notice say the backstage crew would need?
qa.a: The notice said paint, glue, hammers, and no acting.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel while trying to squeeze back into the old group?
qa.a: Vidya felt left out and anxious to fit in, laughing at jokes that made no sense and buying the same keychain, yet still stuck at the end of the bench.

qa.q: What made the backstage crew work where chasing the old group had not?
qa.a: The crew gathered around a shared task, so belonging came from painting and arguing about green together rather than from having to impress anyone.

qa.q: What might it be like for Raghav to have Vidya join the crew?
qa.a: For Raghav, a new pair of hands means the forest gets more trees; handing over a brush with no test was probably an ordinary, welcome thing to do.

grounding: It shows a teen who was left out finding a place in a backstage crew where belonging grows from doing something together.
